BODY CORPORATE NIGHTMARES

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Buying sectional title have several pro's and con's and you should properly weigh up the options before making a decision.

Unique Selling Point:
Buying sectional title have several pro's and con's and you should properly weigh up the options before making a decision.

Sectional title describes the separate ownership of a unit within a group-owned complex or development.
The owner of the unit automatically becomes part of the body corporate, which is the legal entity that owns and controls the common property in the sectional-title scheme. The body corporate lays down the rules that have to be adhered to by all the owners in the development.
In addition, owners are obliged to pay levies according to the size of their units (those with smaller units pay lower levies). These levies are calculated in accordance with a budget, which is prepared annually by the trustees or agent.

WHAT LEVIES ARE NORMALLY FOR:
The levy usually includes the insurance premiums, maintenance of the common property, wages and salaries of cleaners, security and other staff involved in maintaining the common property, as well as any water and electricity required for the common property. Owners of sectional schemes usually only need to pay for their rates and taxes, insurance for the contents of their home, their own private gardens and for their monthly electricity and water consumption. The specifics may differ slightly from complex to complex.

Bodies Corporate have to abide by certain legislation - especially if the body corporate wants to enact rules and regulations not stipulated by the Acts that govern them.
But they often don't follow these procedures, and with most sectional title owners not knowing what their rights are or what the legislation stipulates, they could easily be abused.

BODY CORPORATE RULES: The Sectional Titles Act states that a scheme's rules are binding on the body corporate, the owner of the property and the persons who are occupying the property, that is the tenants.
The rules and regulations of any particular complex may change, and even though all sectional title investors or owners may not necessarily agree with the changes, they would not have the power to change them individually.
Owners of sectional title units also do not have the freedom to alter, renovate or expand their sections without the approval of the body corporate. In addition, all the owners are jointly and separately liable for the debt of the body corporate, which means that if an owner does not pay his/her share, it may become the other owners' problem as well.

In addition, all the owners are jointly and separately liable for the debt of the body corporate, which means that if an owner does not pay his/her share, it may become the other owners' problem as well.


Summary:
BODY CORPORATE RULES: The Sectional Titles Act states that a scheme's rules are binding on the body corporate, the owner of the property and the persons who are occupying the property, that is the tenants.
The rules and regulations of any particular complex may change, and even though all sectional title investors or owners may not necessarily agree with the changes, they would not have the power to change them individually.
Owners of sectional title units also do not have the freedom to alter, renovate or expand their sections without the approval of the body corporate. In addition, all the owners are jointly and separately liable for the debt of the body corporate, which means that if an owner does not pay his/her share, it may become the other owners' problem as well.

There are several advantages as well as disadvantages of buying sectional title homes and prospective buyers need to do their homework in order to make an informed choice.
Once you're in, you are in and you have to abide by the body corporate's management and conduct rules and this of often where war starts to rage...


Further information:
BODY CORPORATE RULES: The Sectional Titles Act states that a scheme's rules are binding on the body corporate, the owner of the property and the persons who are occupying the property, that is the tenants.
In turn, responsibility rests with the owner to ensure that the tenant complies with the rules.

Disputes often happen between owners and body corporates or managing agents over financial issues such as levies, special levies, levies that are in arrears and how the arrears are being collected. This can often created an hostile neighbourly atmosphere.

ADVANTAGES OF BUYING SECTIONAL TITLE:
The popularity of SECTIONAL TITLE homes has grown in over the last decade, not only because they tend to be more cost-effective, but also because they offer heightened security and a more communal way of living. In addition, sectional titles remove the responsibility of having to pay individually for home insurance, and for the upkeep of the communal areas within the complex.
Sectional-title homes are usually more affordable than freestanding properties and provide a good opportunity for young professionals to get a foothold on the property ladder.
Owning a sectional-title unit certainly has its pleasures - you don't have to mow the lawn or clean the swimming pool on Saturday mornings and costs such as insurance, repair and maintenance are shared between owners.

DISADVANTAGES OF BUYING SECTIONAL TITLE:
Living in a sectional title complex can also have its disadvantages. Unlike full-title ownership, where the owner is in complete control and is financially responsible for the property in its entirety, a person who invests in a sectional title scheme will own part of the scheme, meaning that the owner has invested in and is part of a small community.

BOND APPLICATION FOR BUYING SECTIONAL TITLE:

When applying for a bond on a sectional-title property, banks will need to look at the financials of the body corporate, checking what is owed by the scheme, whether loans have been taken to cover  accounts where there have been shortfalls in levies paid, and whether the scheme is  being managed properly and is solvent. Once the bank is satisfied with the financials, the actual purchasing process is like any other. "Your bond will be registered as a sectional-title bond, and the registration and transfer all take place in the same way.

WHAT TO CHECK WHEN BUYING SECTIONAL TITLE:

Over and above the banks' basic  due diligence,buyers must do their own checks too in order to ensure they  know what they are buying into, and how, specifically, these might affect their bond  applications. The Ombud, CSOS, advises that prospective owners of sectional-title properties must scrutinise the budget, the financial statements of the body corporate and the minutes of the meetings held by the trustees of the body corporate for the following reasons:
-You have to ensure that all owners are paying the levies on time. If owners fail to pay the levies the scheme soon falls into disrepair, as the body corporate will not be able to pay its creditors or maintain the building and common property. VO: A large amount owing on arrear levies should immediately trigger a warning bell and might be an indication that the scheme is not managed properly.
- The trustees have to insure the buildings and keep them insured at replacement value. Sectional-title schemes are often under-insured as the trustees fail to increase the insurance on a regular basis, to keep the levies down. The insurance policy has to specify the insured value of each unit. An owner can increase the insured value but will be liable for the additional premium on his or her unit.
- The trustees must establish a fund which is sufficient for the proper upkeep, repair and maintenance of the building and also provide for future expenses. The trustees can also claim payment of special levies to cover specific needs of the scheme. The special levies become payable by owners once a resolution has been taken by the trustees. You should ensure that you will not suddenly have to find the money for an unforeseen special levy. Check the minutes of the meeting of the body corporate and obtain a warranty from the owner from whom you are buying your unit that no special levies are payable, or that the seller will be liable for the payment of such a levy.
- Check everything in the scheme that you are buying into is sound and that the conduct rules are acceptable to you before signing on the dotted line.

PENALTY FEES:

In terms of prescribed Management Rule 25(5) (which is included in the Regulations to the STSMA, and which would apply unless the body corporate has taken a unanimous resolution to amend it as per Regulation 6(6)) a body corporate may not debit an owner’s account with any amount that is not a contribution or a charge levied in terms of the STSMA. Apart from ordinary and special levies and interest thereon, legal fees, and a reasonable photocopy fee for the inspection of documents, no other types of charges are provided for in the legislation itself.

This means that any penalty fee or “administrative” fee or “debt collection” fee charged by a body corporate to an owner, is not authorized by law and would thus be unlawful, unless they are authorized in terms of the scheme’s Conduct or Management Rules. In order for a fine or penalty to be enforceable by a body corporate, it must have been lawfully adopted by the body corporate after the taking of the appropriate resolution, and the amendment to the rules to adopt that fine or penalty must have been registered at the Deeds Office.

There are also rules relating to the way in which the fine is imposed – for example, the imposition of the fine must be reasonable and systematic – the trustees must treat everyone in the scheme equally – and the person being fined must also be given a fair opportunity to state their case to the trustees/managing agent as to why the fine should not be imposed (or else the imposition would not be regarded as reasonable).

INTEREST:

In terms of prescribed Management Rule 21(3)(c) (contained in the Regulations to the STSMA, and which would apply unless the body corporate has taken a unanimous resolution to amend it as per Regulation 6(6))) the trustees of a sectional title body corporate are entitled to charge interest (as they may determine from time to time) on arrear amounts. This interest may only be charged on the authority of a written trustee resolution, and the rate may not exceed the capped rate prescribed by the National Credit Act 34 of 2005 (as amended) (“the NCA”). This interest may be compounded monthly in arrears.

LEGAL COSTS:

Should any of the owners fall into arrears on their account, prescribed Management Rule 25(4) (contained in the Regulations to the STSMA, which will apply unless amended by the body corporate by unanimous resolution) states that an owner of a section will be liable for all reasonable legal costs that the body corporate incurred in recovering the money owed to it by the owner (as taxed or agreed between the body corporate and the owner).

Unfortunately, the STSMA does not explain whether ‘taxed’ means taxed by the Law Society of South Africa or a provincial Law Society, or taxed in terms of the Uniform Rules of the High Court. There is thus some controversy in our law relating to which method of taxing will satisfy the requirements set out in the NCA.

CONCLUSION:

Sectional title bodies corporate can charge interest, provided that it is a maximum of 2% per month compounded and that the trustees have approved the rate in writing (and if necessary the relevant body corporate rules have been amended properly to authorize the levying of such interest) and that the interest charged does not exceed the capital debt or exceed the capital amount;
should legal action be taken by the body corporate to recover the money owed to it, legal fees can only be recovered if such costs were reasonable and agreed to by the defaulting owner, or if the bill was ‘taxed’ (presumably in terms of the Uniform Rules of Court or by a law society or other body with the jurisdiction to tax such bills (such as the Legal Practice Council or one of its provincial councils));
sectional title bodies corporate cannot lawfully impose any other types of charges apart from levies and special levies other than the interest and legal fees referred to above, unless they are authorized by the body corporate’s rules, and they are reasonable, constitutional and applied systematically to everyone. Any other type of charge would be unlawful;
sectional title bodies corporate will most likely be found by our courts not to be subject to the CPA.

Press Release:


Body Corporates

For home buyers, finally owning a property is a dream come true, but sectional title owners can easily find themselves at logger heads with the trustees of their complex’s body corporate – turning a peaceful home into hostile territory. Carte Blanche investigates whether owners know their rights and responsibilities and what to do when they fall foul of trustees and managing agents.

Producer: Stenette Grosskopf and Este de Klerk

Presenter: Derek Watts

Research: Laura Byrne

Script:


BODY CORPORATES SCRIPT
V/O Do you own a property and live in a complex - or a block of flats?
Then you're one of a fast growing number of South Africans who are opting for the affordability, security and commuEnal living that comes along when you buy into a sectional title scheme. It comes with many advantages…
MAIKE GOHL A lot of people consider it to be a lot less lonely to live in a sectional title property
LAUREN SQUIER It allows for people to have their own little unit in the scheme and also share in the common property.
V/O As the saying goes, buying a house is probably the biggest investment most of us will ever make… So, knowing what you're buying into is important -

Because complex living is sometimes… well … complex…

Attorney Izak du Pisani deals with sectional title disputes on a daily basis.
IZAK DU PISANI These days, people with their own social economical backgrounds, the whole cultural diversity being put together in one building does create a situation where there will be confrontation and people being unreasonable. It's colourful. It's a challenge. Somewhere in the middle, you need to try and be fair and reasonable.

Derek: And "MY dogs don't bark!"

Izak: That's the thing, but "At least I've got my recorder on and that is your dogs."
V/O Gloria Lasarow is a pensioner living at Lymington Mews, in Illovo, Johannesburg. She bought the unit 17 years ago and lives with her life-long partner, Norman Donin.
Drowning in debt of hundreds of thousands of rands, the elderly couple is struggling to keep afloat.
GLORIA LASAROW I've been so desperate sometimes that I can't even get out of my room.
DEREK LINK The sad saga started around six years ago when the body corporate insisted that these windows be replaced with a temporary extra levy of R2300.00 a month, charged to each unit.
V/O Besides the monthly levy that every sectional title owner needs to pay towards the upkeep and running costs of the complex, a special levy can also be instituted for necessary maintenance or emergencies.
Lasarow and Donin - already in arrears on their basic levies - refused to pay the added extra special levy.

And so a battle between them and the trustees of the complex's body corporate ensued.
GLORIA LASAROW I said, "We don't need the windows. There's nothing wrong with our windows,"
LAUREN SQUIER Members cannot dispute the special levy based on the fact that they view it to be excessive or unnecessary.
V/O Candidate attorney Lauren Squier, and Property attorney, Maike Gohl are clear that not paying levies is unlawful.
MAIKE GOHL Even if you don't necessarily agree with the levies that are being charged to you, it doesn't matter, you have a legal duty to pay them and the Body Corporate can and will absolutely hold you accountable for those levies.
V/O Lasarow and Donin learned this the hard way. Donin is 85 and still works as a pharmacist - seven days a week - to try and make ends meet, but their financial burden just continues to be too much to bear.
GLORIA LASAROW: They kept sending us accounts and accounts and accounts, with interest and interest, and accounts.
V/O In 2016, Lasarow's outstanding levy account was standing at R97,000. She took the matter on arbitration, but lost the case. She was ordered to pay her outstanding balance, plus interest; as well as almost R140 000 for the legal and arbitration costs.
ISAK DU PISANI [00:11:04.24] It's imperative to make sure that at the time when you are taken to task for the payment of levies, that you educate yourself and make sure that you can handle it, or you go and speak to an attorney. If you can stop it there, it follows that it would have a massive cost-saving implication and all the trouble that comes with it.
GLORIA LASAROW: [00:18:09.13] Derek: Gloria, have you understood all the processes of the law and all the costs, the charges that have been made?

[00:18:18.20] Gloria: How can I? I'm a designer. I've never been with legal complications in my life.
V/O To help resolve disputes like Lasarow's… the Community Schemes Ombud Services - or CSOS - was established in 2016, says acting ombud, Dibuo Rabudi.
NDIVHUO RABULI CSOS is there to say if you have those issues, then you can come to us, then we can intervene and get the body corporate to cooperate and give relevant information or respond to issues.
V/O As a last resort, Lasarow has headed to CSOS where her case is pending. She's disputing several charges added to her account over the years.
DEREK: This must be a big fear of yours, that you could lose your flat?
GLORIA LASAROW: Absolutely. I actually had two nervous breakdowns from this.
V/O Disputes between owners and trustees of the body corporate often also arise because owners ignore or flout the complex's Rules of Conduct.
MAIKE GOHL Conduct rules regulate how people interact with each other in the Body Corporate. They'll have rules like how much noise you can make up until what time and if you're having a party you need to let people know for parking purposes. It's not something to disregard.
LAUREN SQUIER In a lot of cases we see people moving into complexes with dogs, where in the Conduct Rules it clearly states that, "No pets are allowed,"
NAOMI DE CANHA We had a request by someone to have a potbelly pig live on their balcony! Obviously, it is not even a pet animal, it is a farm animal, you can't have that kind of animal living on their second floor balcony.
V/O Naomi de Canha served as the chairperson of the board of trustees at Telford Court in Northriding, Johannesburg for five years.
Trustees are elected by the owners - who form the body corporate - to represent them, and trustees also need to act in the best interest of the complex as a whole.
NAOMI DE CANHA Being a trustee is a very difficult role. Even among the trustees very often you will not find agreement on what is the best way to proceed, let alone in all the owners of the complex.
V/O Especially in a complex such as Telford Court with 293 units.
Sibusiso Ngwenya is the current trustee chairperson at the complex.
Last year, he laid a complaint with CSOS against De Canha as former trustee, two other former trustees and Telford Court's previous managing agent, Body Corporate Assistance, known as BCA.
SIBUSISO NGWENYA I started asking questions long before I was a trustee, with regards to some of the things that were of concern to me.
V/O In 2012, the body corporate voted against a proposed resolution to change the complex's debt collection fee structure.
The trustees proposed to abolish a R75 fixed debt collection fee - and replace it with a R15 fixed fee plus a 10% commission on the arrears amounts to be paid to the managing agent, BCA.
Despite the majority vote not in favour, the Trustees decided to pay the 10% fee to BCA nonetheless.
NAOMI DE CANHA We actually got legal opinion of what was required of us by law - we had to change it irrespective
because owners had voted against the 10% and because we had to do the 10% by law, we didn't charge the 10% to individual accounts at that point, we kept it as a body corporate expense
V/O But Ngwenya says the matter was not handled correctly.
SIBUSISO NGWENYA The money was collected from owner contributions as opposed from the debtor.
NAOMI DE CANHA There is no legal reason why that is incorrect, a body corporate can decide for that to be their policy, or they can decide against it.
V/O Attorney, Maike Gohl disagrees.
MAIKE GOHL The trustees should have been aware that the fees that were being charged weren't lawfully being charged to the Body Corporate and therefore should have not made payment thereof.
V/O In September last year, CSOS ruled in favour of Ngwenya and the Telford Court Body Corporate.
CSOS ordered that De Canha, two fellow former trustees, and BCA were liable - jointly and in their private capacity - to pay back over R300 000 that BCA had been paid as the 10% fee for four years.
The former trustees and BCA rejected the ruling and are appealing.
NAOMI DE CANHA We sought a legal opinion to make sure we didn't do anything wrong.
V/O But as is often the case in body corporate disputes, the conflict between Ngwenya and De Canha escalated way beyond the initial point of contention.
NAOMI DE CANHA It was a very difficult time for all of us.
NAT SOUND
V/O Living in close proximity to your neighbours seems to bring out the worst in some people and in most Body Corporate disputes there are often as many truths as there are owners in a complex…. But when it comes to commuEnal living, experts agree, there are some important lessons to be learnt.
MAIKE GOHL Stick to your conduct rules. Make sure you know what's in them because it can cause a lot of drama and the stupidest -- the silliest fights we see as lawyers, as property lawyers, are neighbour fights.
RABUDI Ask for instance for the audited financial statements of the previous financial year, because that will also assist you in to check the viability - if the scheme is in distress, then you know, more levies that you are going to pay
LAUREN SQUIER Know your rights and your obligations. If you have a dispute, take it to CSOS, take it to the Court. Don't stop paying your levies because once you stop paying your levies you're going to accrue interest and you're going to lose your voice, which is really not beneficial to you.
END

Unlike full-title ownership, where the owner is in complete control and is financially responsible for the property in its entirety, a person who invests in a sectional title scheme will own part of the scheme, meaning that the owner has invested in and is part of a small community. BOND APPLICATION FOR BUYING SECTIONAL TITLE: When applying for a bond on a sectional-title property, banks will need to look at the financials of the body corporate, checking what is owed by the scheme, whether loans have been taken to cover accounts where there have been shortfalls in levies paid, and whether the scheme is being managed properly and is solvent. Once the bank is satisfied with the financials, the actual purchasing process is like any other. "Your bond will be registered as a sectional-title bond, and the registration and transfer all take place in the same way. WHAT TO CHECK WHEN BUYING SECTIONAL TITLE: Over and above the banks' basic due diligence,buyers must do their own checks too in order to ensure they know what they are buying into, and how, specifically, these might affect their bond applications. The Ombud, CSOS, advises that prospective owners of sectional-title properties must scrutinise the budget, the financial statements of the body corporate and the minutes of the meetings held by the trustees of the body corporate for the following reasons: -You have to ensure that all owners are paying the levies on time. If owners fail to pay the levies the scheme soon falls into disrepair, as the body corporate will not be able to pay its creditors or maintain the building and common property. VO: A large amount owing on arrear levies should immediately trigger a warning bell and might be an indication that the scheme is not managed properly. - The trustees have to insure the buildings and keep them insured at replacement value. Sectional-title schemes are often under-insured as the trustees fail to increase the insurance on a regular basis, to keep the levies down. The insurance policy has to specify the insured value of each unit. An owner can increase the insured value but will be liable for the additional premium on his or her unit. - The trustees must establish a fund which is sufficient for the proper upkeep, repair and maintenance of the building and also provide for future expenses. The trustees can also claim payment of special levies to cover specific needs of the scheme. The special levies become payable by owners once a resolution has been taken by the trustees. You should ensure that you will not suddenly have to find the money for an unforeseen special levy. Check the minutes of the meeting of the body corporate and obtain a warranty from the owner from whom you are buying your unit that no special levies are payable, or that the seller will be liable for the payment of such a levy. - Check everything in the scheme that you are buying into is sound and that the conduct rules are acceptable to you before signing on the dotted line. PENALTY FEES: In terms of prescribed Management Rule 25(5) (which is included in the Regulations to the STSMA, and which would apply unless the body corporate has taken a unanimous resolution to amend it as per Regulation 6(6)) a body corporate may not debit an owner’s account with any amount that is not a contribution or a charge levied in terms of the STSMA. Apart from ordinary and special levies and interest thereon, legal fees, and a reasonable photocopy fee for the inspection of documents, no other types of charges are provided for in the legislation itself. This means that any penalty fee or “administrative” fee or “debt collection” fee charged by a body corporate to an owner, is not authorized by law and would thus be unlawful, unless they are authorized in terms of the scheme’s Conduct or Management Rules. In order for a fine or penalty to be enforceable by a body corporate, it must have been lawfully adopted by the body corporate after the taking of the appropriate resolution, and the amendment to the rules to adopt that fine or penalty must have been registered at the Deeds Office. There are also rules relating to the way in which the fine is imposed – for example, the imposition of the fine must be reasonable and systematic – the trustees must treat everyone in the scheme equally – and the person being fined must also be given a fair opportunity to state their case to the trustees/managing agent as to why the fine should not be imposed (or else the imposition would not be regarded as reasonable). INTEREST: In terms of prescribed Management Rule 21(3)(c) (contained in the Regulations to the STSMA, and which would apply unless the body corporate has taken a unanimous resolution to amend it as per Regulation 6(6))) the trustees of a sectional title body corporate are entitled to charge interest (as they may determine from time to time) on arrear amounts. This interest may only be charged on the authority of a written trustee resolution, and the rate may not exceed the capped rate prescribed by the National Credit Act 34 of 2005 (as amended) (“the NCA”). This interest may be compounded monthly in arrears. LEGAL COSTS: Should any of the owners fall into arrears on their account, prescribed Management Rule 25(4) (contained in the Regulations to the STSMA, which will apply unless amended by the body corporate by unanimous resolution) states that an owner of a section will be liable for all reasonable legal costs that the body corporate incurred in recovering the money owed to it by the owner (as taxed or agreed between the body corporate and the owner). Unfortunately, the STSMA does not explain whether ‘taxed’ means taxed by the Law Society of South Africa or a provincial Law Society, or taxed in terms of the Uniform Rules of the High Court. There is thus some controversy in our law relating to which method of taxing will satisfy the requirements set out in the NCA. CONCLUSION: Sectional title bodies corporate can charge interest, provided that it is a maximum of 2% per month compounded and that the trustees have approved the rate in writing (and if necessary the relevant body corporate rules have been amended properly to authorize the levying of such interest) and that the interest charged does not exceed the capital debt or exceed the capital amount; should legal action be taken by the body corporate to recover the money owed to it, legal fees can only be recovered if such costs were reasonable and agreed to by the defaulting owner, or if the bill was ‘taxed’ (presumably in terms of the Uniform Rules of Court or by a law society or other body with the jurisdiction to tax such bills (such as the Legal Practice Council or one of its provincial councils)); sectional title bodies corporate cannot lawfully impose any other types of charges apart from levies and special levies other than the interest and legal fees referred to above, unless they are authorized by the body corporate’s rules, and they are reasonable, constitutional and applied systematically to everyone. Any other type of charge would be unlawful; sectional title bodies corporate will most likely be found by our courts not to be subject to the CPA. Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 31 January 2019 Press Release: Body Corporates For home buyers, finally owning a property is a dream come true, but sectional title owners can easily find themselves at logger heads with the trustees of their complex’s body corporate – turning a peaceful home into hostile territory. Carte Blanche investigates whether owners know their rights and responsibilities and what to do when they fall foul of trustees and managing agents. Producer: Stenette Grosskopf and Este de Klerk Presenter: Derek Watts Research: Laura Byrne Script: BODY CORPORATES SCRIPT V/O Do you own a property and live in a complex - or a block of flats? Then you're one of a fast growing number of South Africans who are opting for the affordability, security and commuEnal living that comes along when you buy into a sectional title scheme. It comes with many advantages… MAIKE GOHL A lot of people consider it to be a lot less lonely to live in a sectional title property LAUREN SQUIER It allows for people to have their own little unit in the scheme and also share in the common property. V/O As the saying goes, buying a house is probably the biggest investment most of us will ever make… So, knowing what you're buying into is important - Because complex living is sometimes… well … complex… Attorney Izak du Pisani deals with sectional title disputes on a daily basis. IZAK DU PISANI These days, people with their own social economical backgrounds, the whole cultural diversity being put together in one building does create a situation where there will be confrontation and people being unreasonable. It's colourful. It's a challenge. Somewhere in the middle, you need to try and be fair and reasonable. Derek: And "MY dogs don't bark!" Izak: That's the thing, but "At least I've got my recorder on and that is your dogs." V/O Gloria Lasarow is a pensioner living at Lymington Mews, in Illovo, Johannesburg. She bought the unit 17 years ago and lives with her life-long partner, Norman Donin. Drowning in debt of hundreds of thousands of rands, the elderly couple is struggling to keep afloat. GLORIA LASAROW I've been so desperate sometimes that I can't even get out of my room. DEREK LINK The sad saga started around six years ago when the body corporate insisted that these windows be replaced with a temporary extra levy of R2300.00 a month, charged to each unit. V/O Besides the monthly levy that every sectional title owner needs to pay towards the upkeep and running costs of the complex, a special levy can also be instituted for necessary maintenance or emergencies. Lasarow and Donin - already in arrears on their basic levies - refused to pay the added extra special levy. And so a battle between them and the trustees of the complex's body corporate ensued. GLORIA LASAROW I said, "We don't need the windows. There's nothing wrong with our windows," LAUREN SQUIER Members cannot dispute the special levy based on the fact that they view it to be excessive or unnecessary. V/O Candidate attorney Lauren Squier, and Property attorney, Maike Gohl are clear that not paying levies is unlawful. MAIKE GOHL Even if you don't necessarily agree with the levies that are being charged to you, it doesn't matter, you have a legal duty to pay them and the Body Corporate can and will absolutely hold you accountable for those levies. V/O Lasarow and Donin learned this the hard way. Donin is 85 and still works as a pharmacist - seven days a week - to try and make ends meet, but their financial burden just continues to be too much to bear. GLORIA LASAROW: They kept sending us accounts and accounts and accounts, with interest and interest, and accounts. V/O In 2016, Lasarow's outstanding levy account was standing at R97,000. She took the matter on arbitration, but lost the case. She was ordered to pay her outstanding balance, plus interest; as well as almost R140 000 for the legal and arbitration costs. ISAK DU PISANI [00:11:04.24] It's imperative to make sure that at the time when you are taken to task for the payment of levies, that you educate yourself and make sure that you can handle it, or you go and speak to an attorney. If you can stop it there, it follows that it would have a massive cost-saving implication and all the trouble that comes with it. GLORIA LASAROW: [00:18:09.13] Derek: Gloria, have you understood all the processes of the law and all the costs, the charges that have been made? [00:18:18.20] Gloria: How can I? I'm a designer. I've never been with legal complications in my life. V/O To help resolve disputes like Lasarow's… the Community Schemes Ombud Services - or CSOS - was established in 2016, says acting ombud, Dibuo Rabudi. NDIVHUO RABULI CSOS is there to say if you have those issues, then you can come to us, then we can intervene and get the body corporate to cooperate and give relevant information or respond to issues. V/O As a last resort, Lasarow has headed to CSOS where her case is pending. She's disputing several charges added to her account over the years. DEREK: This must be a big fear of yours, that you could lose your flat? GLORIA LASAROW: Absolutely. I actually had two nervous breakdowns from this. V/O Disputes between owners and trustees of the body corporate often also arise because owners ignore or flout the complex's Rules of Conduct. MAIKE GOHL Conduct rules regulate how people interact with each other in the Body Corporate. They'll have rules like how much noise you can make up until what time and if you're having a party you need to let people know for parking purposes. It's not something to disregard. LAUREN SQUIER In a lot of cases we see people moving into complexes with dogs, where in the Conduct Rules it clearly states that, "No pets are allowed," NAOMI DE CANHA We had a request by someone to have a potbelly pig live on their balcony! Obviously, it is not even a pet animal, it is a farm animal, you can't have that kind of animal living on their second floor balcony. V/O Naomi de Canha served as the chairperson of the board of trustees at Telford Court in Northriding, Johannesburg for five years. Trustees are elected by the owners - who form the body corporate - to represent them, and trustees also need to act in the best interest of the complex as a whole. NAOMI DE CANHA Being a trustee is a very difficult role. Even among the trustees very often you will not find agreement on what is the best way to proceed, let alone in all the owners of the complex. V/O Especially in a complex such as Telford Court with 293 units. Sibusiso Ngwenya is the current trustee chairperson at the complex. Last year, he laid a complaint with CSOS against De Canha as former trustee, two other former trustees and Telford Court's previous managing agent, Body Corporate Assistance, known as BCA. SIBUSISO NGWENYA I started asking questions long before I was a trustee, with regards to some of the things that were of concern to me. V/O In 2012, the body corporate voted against a proposed resolution to change the complex's debt collection fee structure. The trustees proposed to abolish a R75 fixed debt collection fee - and replace it with a R15 fixed fee plus a 10% commission on the arrears amounts to be paid to the managing agent, BCA. Despite the majority vote not in favour, the Trustees decided to pay the 10% fee to BCA nonetheless. NAOMI DE CANHA We actually got legal opinion of what was required of us by law - we had to change it irrespective because owners had voted against the 10% and because we had to do the 10% by law, we didn't charge the 10% to individual accounts at that point, we kept it as a body corporate expense V/O But Ngwenya says the matter was not handled correctly. SIBUSISO NGWENYA The money was collected from owner contributions as opposed from the debtor. NAOMI DE CANHA There is no legal reason why that is incorrect, a body corporate can decide for that to be their policy, or they can decide against it. V/O Attorney, Maike Gohl disagrees. MAIKE GOHL The trustees should have been aware that the fees that were being charged weren't lawfully being charged to the Body Corporate and therefore should have not made payment thereof. V/O In September last year, CSOS ruled in favour of Ngwenya and the Telford Court Body Corporate. CSOS ordered that De Canha, two fellow former trustees, and BCA were liable - jointly and in their private capacity - to pay back over R300 000 that BCA had been paid as the 10% fee for four years. The former trustees and BCA rejected the ruling and are appealing. NAOMI DE CANHA We sought a legal opinion to make sure we didn't do anything wrong. V/O But as is often the case in body corporate disputes, the conflict between Ngwenya and De Canha escalated way beyond the initial point of contention. NAOMI DE CANHA It was a very difficult time for all of us. NAT SOUND V/O Living in close proximity to your neighbours seems to bring out the worst in some people and in most Body Corporate disputes there are often as many truths as there are owners in a complex…. But when it comes to commuEnal living, experts agree, there are some important lessons to be learnt. MAIKE GOHL Stick to your conduct rules. Make sure you know what's in them because it can cause a lot of drama and the stupidest -- the silliest fights we see as lawyers, as property lawyers, are neighbour fights. RABUDI Ask for instance for the audited financial statements of the previous financial year, because that will also assist you in to check the viability - if the scheme is in distress, then you know, more levies that you are going to pay LAUREN SQUIER Know your rights and your obligations. If you have a dispute, take it to CSOS, take it to the Court. Don't stop paying your levies because once you stop paying your levies you're going to accrue interest and you're going to lose your voice, which is really not beneficial to you. END PROMOS PROMO 10" VO: Owning your own property feels like a great investment - and it does come with many advantages. VO: But do you, as a homeowner know your rights and responsibilities and what to do when you fall foul of trustees and managing agents. LAUREN: If you have a dispute, take it to CSOS, take it to the Court. Don't stop paying your levies

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Buying sectional title have several pro's and con's and you should properly weigh up the options before making a decision. Sectional title describes the separate ownership of a unit within a group-owned complex or development. The owner of the unit automatically becomes part of the body corporate, which is the legal entity that owns and controls the common property in the sectional-title scheme. The body corporate lays down the rules that have to be adhered to by all the owners in the development. In addition, owners are obliged to pay levies according to the size of their units (those with smaller units pay lower levies). These levies are calculated in accordance with a budget, which is prepared annually by the trustees or agent. WHAT LEVIES ARE NORMALLY FOR: The levy usually includes the insurance premiums, maintenance of the common property, wages and salaries of cleaners, security and other staff involved in maintaining the common property, as well as any water and electricity required for the common property. Owners of sectional schemes usually only need to pay for their rates and taxes, insurance for the contents of their home, their own private gardens and for their monthly electricity and water consumption. The specifics may differ slightly from complex to complex. Bodies Corporate have to abide by certain legislation - especially if the body corporate wants to enact rules and regulations not stipulated by the Acts that govern them. But they often don't follow these procedures, and with most sectional title owners not knowing what their rights are or what the legislation stipulates, they could easily be abused. BODY CORPORATE RULES: The Sectional Titles Act states that a scheme's rules are binding on the body corporate, the owner of the property and the persons who are occupying the property, that is the tenants. The rules and regulations of any particular complex may change, and even though all sectional title investors or owners may not necessarily agree with the changes, they would not have the power to change them individually. Owners of sectional title units also do not have the freedom to alter, renovate or expand their sections without the approval of the body corporate. In addition, all the owners are jointly and separately liable for the debt of the body corporate, which means that if an owner does not pay his/her share, it may become the other owners' problem as well.
